ROI Background Methods

How anytrack estimates each arena's background for detection, the three methods available, and how they compare on 8 real localsearch clips (2176×2176, 4 arenas, ~18 000 frames). The background is the plate that every frame is subtracted from, so its quality sets the ceiling on centroid tracking.

Analysis date: 2026-07-06 · companion to streaming_bg_parity.html & pipeline.html
Context. The parity fix solved the start bake-in (a fly still at frame 0). The residual limit is dwell contamination: where a fly rests for a large fraction of the clip, its dark body / bright optical halo leaks into that pixel's background estimate, leaving a patch that no longer matches the true arena. When the fly later moves, background subtraction lights that patch up as a ghost candidate — a second fly-like blob the centroid tracker can latch onto. These three methods are increasingly aggressive at removing that contamination.

1 · The three methods

gmm — brighter-component Gaussian mixture current default

Per pixel, fit a 1–2 component Gaussian mixture (vectorised numpy EM) to the sampled brightness and take the brighter component as the background (arena is bright, fly is dark). Robust to the fly appearing in a minority of frames, and — with uniform sampling — to the start bake-in. Weakness: at a dwell pixel the bright-component estimate is supported by few arena samples and can be biased by the resting fly's halo, leaving a patch slightly brighter (or darker) than the true arena. background.py: fit_gmm_background. Cost: the GMM fit (already ~12× faster than sklearn).

percentile — per-pixel high percentile simple, robust

Background = per-pixel p% (here p90) of the sampled brightness. For a dark fly on a bright arena the arena is the high-brightness value, so p90 recovers it as long as the arena is visible in at least ~10% of samples (dwell up to ~90%). It cannot overshoot brighter than an actually-observed arena pixel, so it can't invent a bright ghost patch the way a fitted mixture can. Cheapest of the three (one np.percentile); no model to diverge. Weakness: at a true >90%-dwell pixel it still sees the fly.

fg_excluded — percentile with the fly masked out cleanest

Track the fly once (on a percentile background), then rebuild each pixel's background as the percentile over only the samples in which the tracked fly is far from that pixel (a disk around the fly is masked out of every sample). The arena estimate never sees the fly, so dwell ghosts vanish entirely; pixels the fly always covers fall back to the plain percentile. Cost: one extra tracking pass (chicken-and-egg: needs a provisional track). preprocess-style masking in gui/debug_app._bg_fg_excluded.

2 · Quantitative comparison — candidate ambiguity

The symptom that matters is multiple fly-like candidates in one arena: when background subtraction lights up more than one blob, the centroid tracker (no appearance model) can pick the wrong one. So we run the real detector (extract_ellipses) against each method's background over 60 frames per clip and count candidates. Aggregated over all 32 arena-cells:

methodmean candidates / frame frames with ≥2 (ambiguous)coverage (≥1)
gmm2.0454.8%100.0%
percentile0.920.0%91.8%
fg_excluded1.000.0%99.6%
gmm is the source of the multi-candidate problem — it averages ~2 candidates/frame and produces ≥2 in ~55% of frames. Its brighter-component estimate leaves faint dwell/halo residue that clears the detection threshold as a second blob. percentile and fg_excluded both drop that to 0% ambiguity; the difference is coverage — percentile misses the fly on ~8% of frames (heavy-dwell pixels where even p90 sees the fly), while fg_excluded holds ~99.6% coverage.

Per-arena multi-candidate rate (% of frames with ≥2 candidates). red > 20%, green = 0%.

A note on "brighter patches". A center-disk measurement of background brightness at the fly's most-dwelt pixel comes out darker than the arena, not brighter — because that pixel is usually the persistent dark center fixture (baked into every background) or a fully-baked-in rest spot. The bright residue you see in the GUI is the fly's halo ring around that dark core; it's faint, so a per-pixel brightness metric understates it — but the candidate count above captures its real effect directly.

3 · Visual results — per-video backgrounds

Each grid: rows = arenas, columns = gmm / percentile / fg_excluded. The methods agree where the fly roams; they diverge at dwell spots. The persistent dark dot present in all three columns is a fixed fixture (not a fly), so no background method removes it.

4 · Recommendation

Adopt fg_excluded — it is the only method that both eliminates the multi-candidate ambiguity (0% vs gmm's ~55%) and keeps coverage high (~99.6%), at the cost of one extra tracking pass. Where that pass isn't affordable, percentile is the low-cost fallback (0% ambiguity too, but ~8% of frames lose the fly on heavy-dwell pixels). gmm should be retired for this assay — it is what generates the competing candidates. Next step: port fg_excluded into the production pipeline (preprocess.build_roi_backgrounds_uniform, two-pass: percentile → track → mask → refit) behind a config switch, and optionally add the tracker contrast-gate as a cheap belt-and-suspenders ghost filter.

5 · Reproduce

All backgrounds and metrics come from the anytrack-debug core, so they match the GUI's background selector exactly. In anytrack-debug <video>, the Experiments (dwell) panel switches background method live and re-tracks, and the candidates pane annotates each blob's contrast so you can watch a ghost appear/disappear per method. Grids: generate_bg_methods.py; metrics: measure_bg_methods.py (dwell excess from the v3 tracks).
